first_message: Everyone thinks of the mean as the central tendency or average, but explain what it is for the mean to be a model?

user_input: I predict the new data point fits with the typical pattern, meaning the new data point is close in value to the mean.
current_question: That makes sense as a prediction strategy. Now, when a real data point isn't exactly equal to the mean, what would you call that difference, and what does it tell us about the model?

user_input: I would call the difference the residual, and if the residual is smaller, it means the model better predicts that data point.
current_question: Good. Now think about this at the level of the whole dataset, not just one point. If I have 100 data points, each with its own residual, how would you combine all of these residuals into one overall measure of how well the mean is doing as a model?

user_input: Well the mean is a balancing point for residuals, so even if the residuals are large, they are equal to each side of the mean and sum to zero. user_input: Yes, if there are outliers in my data, my model might not be as good as predicting where the majority of the spread of data is
